segments.english: When the sun had set and it was thick darkness, there was a smoking furnace and a flaming torch that passed between these pieces.
segments.literal: and-was the-sun came and-thick-darkness was and-behold furnace-of smoke and-torch-of fire which passed between the-pieces the-these

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; introduces a circumstantial clause, here rendered by 'When'
perfect (qatal), 3rd feminine singular, accented on the first syllable (mil'el); of the sun 'go in' = 'set' (Rashi: שָׁקְעָה)
perfect (qatal), 3rd masculine singular, after its feminine subject עֲלָטָה: the clause is impersonal, 'it was thick darkness' (Rashi: חָשַׁךְ הַיּוֹם)
גֶּזֶר, a part cut off; the plural is the halves of the animals cut in v. 10 (בְּתָרִים). Elsewhere only Ps 136:13 (לִגְזָרִים, the sea cut into parts)

phrases.literal: 'and-was the-sun came'; Rashi: וַיְהִי דָּבָר זֶה, a circumstantial clause, and בָּאָה = שָׁקְעָה
'and-behold furnace-of smoke'; הִנֵּה marks what Abram sees; Radak takes עָשָׁן as an adjective, 'a furnace that smoked'

grammar: וַיְהִי opens a time clause; both clauses that follow put the subject before the verb: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בָּאָה, וַעֲלָטָה הָיָה (Rashi: וַיְהִי דָּבָר זֶה, 'and this thing happened').
בָּאָה is accented on the first syllable (zaqef qaton on a mil'el form), so it is a perfect, 'had come', not a participle 'is coming' (Rashi, Radak).
הָיָה is masculine although עֲלָטָה is feminine; the clause is impersonal: 'it was thick darkness'.
תַּנּוּר and לַפִּיד are in the construct before עָשָׁן and אֵשׁ; Radak reads עָשָׁן as an adjective ('a smoky furnace').
אֲשֶׁר עָבַר is singular after two nouns. That fits one apparition, a smoking furnace with the torch inside it (Ibn Ezra, Ramban); Radak has the torch pass between the pieces.
The etnaḥta on הָיָה divides the scene (sunset, darkness) from the vision.
segments.note: Followed Rashi (and Radak) on בָּאָה: a perfect, the sun had set. Ibn Ezra agrees: in v. 12 (לָבוֹא) the sun had not yet set, and here it has. עֲלָטָה is a thick darkness. The verb עָבַר is singular: for Ibn Ezra and Ramban one figure passes, a furnace with a torch of fire inside it; Radak has the torch pass, to confirm the covenant of the next verse.

commentary.summary: Rashi: ויהי השמש באה is like 'and it came to pass, they were emptying their sacks' (Gen 42:35), i.e. 'and this thing happened': a circumstantial clause.
Rashi: השמש באה means שָׁקְעָה, the sun set.
Rashi: ועלטה היה means the day grew dark.
Rashi: the furnace of smoke hints that the kingdoms will fall into Gehenna; homiletic, not the plain sense of the words.

Rashi: the accent being on the upper (first) syllable, בָּאָה is perfect, 'had already come'; with the accent below it would be a participle 'was setting', but the passage of the furnace came afterwards, so the sun had already set. The same holds for words like בָּא, קָם, שָׁב.
Ibn Ezra: 'at first' (v. 12) the sun had not yet set, as לָבוֹא is written there; here בָּאָה means that it has set. He agrees with Rashi.
Ibn Ezra: עלטה is darkness, as in Ezekiel; either the night was clouded or it means the time after the visible light in the clouds.
Ibn Ezra: it was in the likeness of a furnace from which smoke rises, with a torch of fire in it.
Ibn Ezra: בין הגזרים is בין הבתרים, 'between the pieces', and this is the oath, like 'the calf they cut in two' (Jer 34:18); hence 'On that day the LORD made a covenant' follows.
Ramban: the smoking furnace is the cloud and fog of Sinai and the torch the fire from which Israel heard the words; the Presence itself passed between the pieces, which is the covenant.

Radak: the passing between the pieces signals the covenant-making, as parties passed between halved animals; the torch stands for God, and also hints at the fire that will consume the nations of the exile.

apparatus: גֶּזֶר: the plural גְּזָרִים occurs elsewhere only in Ps 136:13; Ibn Ezra and Radak equate it with the בְּתָרִים of v. 10.

segments.english: On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your offspring I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
segments.literal: in-the-day the-that cut the-LORD with-Abram covenant to-say to-your-seed I-have-given the-land the-this from-river-of Egypt until the-river the-great river-of Euphrates

tokens.note: idiom: כרת ברית, 'cut a covenant'
the divine name יְהוָה (written יְהֹוָה in MAM)
the pack parses אֶת־ here as a preposition, 'with'; it is the preposition אֵת with Abram
infinitive construct with ל, introduces direct speech
ל + זֶרַע + 2ms suffix
perfect: Rashi, the divine word as if already done
spatial 'as far as' (BDB sense I, not printed in the pack; II.1 is temporal 'until')
attributive adjective with the article, 'great' in size (BDB sense 1, not printed in the pack; 4 is 'loud'); Rashi: called great because it adjoins the Land of Israel

phrases.english: the LORD made a covenant with Abram
phrases.literal: 'cut the-LORD with-Abram covenant'; כרת ברית is 'cut a covenant'

phrases.english: To your offspring I have given
phrases.literal: 'to-your-seed I-have-given'; the perfect נָתַתִּי states a future gift as accomplished (Rashi, Radak)
'(OBJ) the-land the-this'; אֶת is the object marker and has no English counterpart
'from-river-of Egypt'; Ibn Ezra: the Shiḥor, not the Nile

phrases.english: to the great river, the river Euphrates

grammar: כָּרַת בְּרִית is the idiom 'cut a covenant'; the verb's basic sense is 'cut' (cf. the pieces of v. 17).
לֵאמֹר (ל + infinitive construct of אמר) introduces the speech; לְזַרְעֲךָ stands before its verb, which puts the weight on 'to your offspring'.
נָתַתִּי is a perfect of certainty: the promise is spoken as already given (Rashi: the saying of the Holy One is as if done).
מִנְּהַר מִצְרַיִם עַד־הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל: the boundaries are given as two rivers; נְהַר־פְּרָת stands in apposition to 'the great river'.
יְהֹוָה is read 'the LORD' (decisions).
segments.note: 'I have given' keeps the perfect. נְהַר מִצְרַיִם is rendered 'the river of Egypt' because Ibn Ezra identifies it as the Shiḥor and not the Nile (היאור); the Hebrew word is unchanged. The token אֶת־ at 15:18.5 is parsed as a preposition (BDB a.gn.aa, 'with'): kept as given, the sense list of that entry has 'together with' but Abram here is the party with whom the covenant is cut, so 'with' is the reading.

commentary.summary: Rashi: לזרעך נתתי, the saying of the Holy One is as if it were already done.
Rashi: it is called 'great' because it adjoins the Land of Israel, although it is last of the four rivers from Eden ('and the fourth river is the Perat'); proverb: 'a king's servant is a king'.
Ibn Ezra: נהר מצרים is the Shiḥor and not the Nile (היאור).

Ramban: God promised Abraham the land several times, each time adding to it; here the borders and the ten nations are named and a covenant is made so that sin will not annul the gift. The earlier promises say אֶתֵּן (future), but at the covenant he says נָתַתִּי, for the covenant is made on a gift already given; Rashi's 'as if done' is not needed here.
Radak: נתתי means 'I have already given them by my word, which stands.'

apparatus: Ibn Ezra: 'river of Egypt' = the Shiḥor, not the Nile.
Onkelos: לִבְנָךְ יְהָבִית, 'to your son(s) I have given'; 'the great river' as נַהֲרָא רַבָּא.

segments.english: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites;

tokens.note: gentilic singular, used collectively
gentilic singular, collective
BDB: Easterners; a people named, from קֶדֶם 'east'

phrases.literal: object of נָתַתִּי in v. 18; the gentilic is singular and collective

grammar: The verse continues the list of objects of נָתַתִּי (v. 18); each name is a singular gentilic with the article, read collectively.
Each name after the first takes וְאֵת, 'and (object marker)'.
The pashta and zaqef qaton divide the three names; the silluq closes the verse.
segments.note: קַדְמֹנִי is 'Kadmonites' (BDB 'Easterners'), a name for a people, kept as a name. The list of names resumes in v. 20.

commentary.summary: Rashi: there are ten nations here but only seven were given; the three, Kenite, Kenizzite and Kadmonite, correspond to Edom, Moab and Ammon and will be an inheritance in the future (Gen. Rabbah).
Ibn Ezra: these are from the sons of Canaan, and they have two names (each of the three was also known by another name).

Radak: the Kenites are named after the city they first lived in, Kayin (Judg 4:11), perhaps named after its builder; the family intermarried with the tribe of Judah, with the families of Rechab (1 Chr 2:55).
Radak, continuing 15:19:1: perhaps the Kenite named here is a different people from the Kenite clan he has just described; but Onkelos renders it שַׁלְמָאֵי, as he renders the Kenite of Num 24:21.

segments.english: the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim;

tokens.note: gentilic singular, collective
gentilic singular, collective
plural gentilic; also the name of the giants' people

grammar: The list continues with the objects of נָתַתִּי; the ו of each וְאֶת is rendered by the commas and the final 'and'.
הַחִתִּי, הַפְּרִזִּי are singular collective gentilics; הָרְפָאִים is plural.
The merkha, tipḥa and silluq accents mark the three names.
segments.note: רְפָאִים is kept as 'Rephaim'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra identify it with the land of Og ('the land of Rephaim', Deut 3:13). Ibn Ezra explains that the ten nations are all Canaanite in a wide sense.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the Rephaim are the land of Og, of which it is said 'that too is called the land of Rephaim' (Deut 3:13).

Ibn Ezra: this is the 'land of Rephaim' of Deut 3:13. Do not wonder that the Canaanite and the Jebusite follow: the seven nations are all Canaanites, Canaan had eleven sons, and after six are named 'the Canaanite' covers the rest; here the nations are listed one by one, elsewhere as a whole, as 'Judah and Israel' (1 Kgs 4:20) although Judah is part of Israel.
Radak: the Hivite is not named in this list; perhaps it is the Rephaim that is named (the comment continues at radak:15:20:2).
Radak, ending 15:20:1: the Hivite, missing from the list, is perhaps 'the Rephaim that he named' (הָרְפָאִים שֶׁזָּכַר).

apparatus: Onkelos renders הרפאים as גִּבָּרָאֵי, 'the mighty'.

segments.english: the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.

grammar: The final four names of the ten; the paragraph mark (ס) closes the section.
All are singular gentilics read as collectives.
The pashta, zaqef qaton and tipḥa divide the four names in pairs; the silluq ends the verse.
segments.note: The paragraph mark ס follows the verse. 'Canaanites' here is the narrower people, as the other nations are also Canaan's descendants (Ibn Ezra, v. 20).

commentary.summary: Radak: the land of the Philistines is included in 'the Canaanite', as Joshua says 'it is counted to the Canaanite' (Josh 13:3).
